cards.body: It's 11 pm. You're done for the day, but your mind isn't. It replays a conversation, checks tomorrow for problems, then starts again from the top. You didn't decide to do this. It just happens.

cards.title: It's not a flaw in you
cards.body: That late-night spin can feel like proof that something is wrong with you. It's more ordinary than that. Your brain is doing something it has practiced many times, the same way your hand reaches for your phone without asking you first.

cards.title: Anxiety can run on autopilot
cards.body: A lot of anxiety works like a habit. Something sets it off, you respond in a familiar way, and you get a brief payoff. Each time the cycle repeats, it gets a little more automatic.

cards.title: Habits can be relearned
cards.body: The good news about habits is that they were learned, so they can be relearned. You don't need to force the anxiety away. Over the next 30 days you'll learn to see the cycle clearly, and that alone starts to loosen it.

cards.title: Just to be safe
cards.body: Priya checks her work inbox every evening "just to be safe." Most nights she finds nothing urgent, yet she feels tense for an hour afterward. Checking has become a habit that promises calm and rarely delivers it.
Think of one moment this week when worry switched on by itself. Where were you? What time was it? Just picture it. There's nothing to fix yet.

cards.title: Catch worry switching on
cards.body: Sometime today, notice one moment when worry starts up on its own. You don't need to do anything about it. Just say to yourself, "There it is."
cards.footer: Loosening Worry is a self-help course, not a treatment or a diagnosis. If anxiety is making daily life very hard, or you're in crisis, open Help for support lines.

cards.body: You unlock your phone to check the time. Ten minutes later you're deep in a feed, and you still don't know what time it is.

cards.title: Three parts, every time
cards.body: Habits run as small loops with three parts. A **trigger** sets it off: a place, a feeling, a thought. A **behavior** follows: the thing you do. Then comes a **result**: what you get, or what you feel, right afterward.

cards.title: The result keeps it going
cards.body: Your brain watches the result closely. If the behavior brought even a moment of relief, distraction or comfort, your brain files it as "worth repeating." Next time the trigger shows up, the behavior is a little quicker to follow.

cards.title: Seeing the parts is step one
cards.body: Most loops run too fast to notice. Breaking one into its three parts slows it down, so you can see what's actually happening instead of just being carried along.

cards.title: "Got a minute?"
cards.body: Sam's manager sends a short message: "Got a minute?" (trigger). Sam spends the next half hour imagining what went wrong (behavior). Sam feels drained and on edge, and the meeting turns out to be about holiday dates (result).
Pick the phone example or one of your own. Say each part to yourself: "The trigger was… I did… Afterwards I felt…"

cards.title: Log your first loop
cards.body: When you catch one today, tap Log and choose a trigger, a behavior and a result. It doesn't need to be a worry loop yet. Any habit counts.
You've read the email five times. Nothing in it has changed, but you're still searching it for a hidden meaning.

cards.title: Feeling vs. doing
cards.body: Anxiety often arrives as a feeling: a tight chest, a fluttery stomach. Worry is what we tend to *do* next. We replay, rehearse, predict and check. It feels like it's happening to us, but it's an action the mind takes.

cards.title: Worry fits the loop
cards.body: That means worry can sit in the behavior slot of a loop. An uneasy feeling is the trigger. Worrying is the behavior. The result is often more unease, which becomes the trigger for the next round.

cards.title: Why this helps
cards.body: You can't simply switch a feeling off. But you can notice a behavior, and a behavior you notice is one you have some choice about. Calling worry a behavior gives you somewhere to start.

cards.title: No reply yet
cards.body: Leo feels a twinge of unease when his friend doesn't reply to a text (trigger). He scrolls back through the chat, guessing what he said wrong (behavior). He ends up more uneasy than before, and checks again (result).
Think of a recent worry. Instead of asking "What was I worried about?", ask "What was I *doing*?" Replaying? Planning for the worst? Checking? Pick the word that fits.

cards.title: Log one worry loop
cards.body: Log one loop where worrying is the behavior. If you're not sure, choose "Overthought it" and keep going. A rough log is better than none.
Sunday evening rolls around and your mood drops, even though nothing bad has happened yet. The week ahead hasn't started, but your body already knows it's coming.

cards.title: Triggers are everywhere
cards.body: A trigger is anything that sets a loop in motion. Some are outside you: a place, a time of day, a notification, a person's name on the screen. Others are inside: a thought, a memory, a sensation like a racing heart.

cards.title: They're often small
cards.body: Triggers are rarely dramatic. A single word in a message, the sound of keys in the door, or simply feeling tired can be enough. Because they're small, they slip past us, and the loop seems to start from nowhere.

cards.title: Spotting them gives you a head start
cards.body: When you know your common triggers, they stop being ambushes. You can see one coming and think, "Ah, this is where it usually starts." That moment of recognition is where change begins.

cards.title: Three start points
cards.body: Maya noticed her worry loops cluster at three points: opening her banking app, the walk into the office, and lying down at night. Seeing the pattern helped her realize the worry wasn't random. It had regular start points.
Scan your day so far. Pick one trigger from each group if you can: a **place**, a **time**, a **person**, a **thought**. Don't judge them. Just name them.

cards.title: Note 3 triggers you noticed today
cards.body: Notice three triggers today. Log each one when you catch it, and pick your best guess for the behavior and result. The trigger is today's focus.
The night before a flight, you mentally run through everything that could go wrong. Somehow it feels irresponsible *not* to.

cards.title: Worry makes a promise
cards.body: Worry sticks around because it seems to offer something. It promises that if you think hard enough, you'll be ready, you'll stay safe, or you won't be caught off guard. That promise is the payoff your brain is chasing.

cards.title: Feeling in control isn't being in control
cards.body: While you're worrying, you feel busy and alert, as if you're handling the problem. But most of the time nothing actually gets solved. The plane flies the same whether you worry or not. You just arrive more tired.

cards.title: Name the promise
cards.body: You don't have to argue with worry. Start by asking what it's promising you this time: Safety? Being prepared? Avoiding blame? Once you can name the promise, you can start checking whether it keeps it.

cards.title: Twenty useful minutes
cards.body: Aisha worries about her presentation every evening for a week. She tells herself it's preparation. When she looks back, the useful part took 20 minutes: writing her notes. The other six evenings were replays that left her no more ready.
Think of a recent worry. Finish this sentence: "If I keep worrying about this, then…" Whatever comes next is the promise.

cards.title: Log a loop and name what you hoped worry would do
cards.body: Log a worry loop, then add a note naming what you hoped the worry would do for you. Keep it to a few words, like "keep me safe" or "be ready."
The letter from the bank has been on the counter for a week. You haven't opened it. Every time you walk past, your stomach tightens a little.

cards.title: Avoiding is a behavior too
cards.body: Not every loop is busy thinking. Sometimes the behavior is stepping away: not opening the message, leaving the call for later, changing the subject. It can look like doing nothing, but it fills the behavior slot just the same.

cards.title: The relief is real, and short
cards.body: Putting something off brings a quick wave of relief. Your brain files that relief as the result, which is why avoiding feels so right in the moment. But the thing you avoided is still there, and so is the worry about it, often a little bigger.

cards.title: Look at the whole result
cards.body: The trick is to look past the first few seconds. What did avoiding give you an hour later? A day later? When you see the full result, not just the first moment of relief, the loop starts to lose its pull.

cards.title: The unanswered invite
cards.body: Tom's friend invites him to a party where he'll know almost no one (trigger). He leaves the message unanswered for three days (behavior). Each day brings a small relief, then a bigger knot of guilt, and by the weekend the reply feels harder to write than ever (result).
Think of one thing you've been putting off. Ask yourself: "What did avoiding it give me right away? And what has it given me since?" Notice both answers.

cards.title: Log one thing you put off
cards.body: Log one loop where you avoided something or put it off. Choose "Avoided it" or "Put it off." For the result, pick what it gave you later, not just in the first minute.
One loop on its own looks random. A week of them starts to look like a map.

cards.title: Each log is a dot
cards.body: Every loop you've logged is a dot on a map. One dot doesn't say much. A handful start to show where your loops tend to begin, and when.

cards.title: Look for repeats
cards.body: Most people find their loops cluster: the same two or three triggers, the same time of day, the same habit stepping in. These repeats are your most practiced loops, which makes them the most useful to know.

cards.title: Curious, not critical
cards.body: A map is just information. A busy week of loops doesn't mean you're doing badly. It means you're noticing more, which is exactly the skill this course builds.

cards.title: Where the worry lives
cards.body: After a week of logging, Mei opened Insights and saw that most of her loops started between 9 and 11 pm, and "Kept checking" came up again and again. She hadn't realized her evenings were where most of the worry lived.
Before you look, make a guess. Which trigger do you think shows up most? What time of day? Hold your guess in mind.

cards.title: Review your loops in Insights
cards.body: Open Insights and look at your week. Check your guess against what's there: your top triggers, when loops tend to start, and what your most common habit gave you. If you've logged only a few loops, that's fine. Look at what's there.
It's 4 pm, a hard email has just landed, and you find yourself standing at the fridge. You're not really hungry.

cards.title: Anxiety wears disguises
cards.body: Worry isn't the only habit that grows from unease. Scrolling, snacking, tidying, over-planning, a quick search online: any of these can step in when something feels uncomfortable.

cards.title: Same loop, different behavior
cards.body: The shape is the same. A trigger brings unease, the behavior offers a quick change of feeling, and the result is what you get. The behavior may look harmless, even pleasant, but it's running the same loop.

cards.title: Not bad, just a loop
cards.body: This isn't about cutting out snacks or your phone. It's about seeing when a habit is doing a job for your anxiety. Once you see the job, you can check how well it does it.

cards.title: A cookie for every email
cards.body: Whenever a hard email landed, Priya went to the kitchen for a cookie. She wasn't hungry; it just took the edge off. Ten minutes later the email was still waiting, and she felt a little sluggish on top of the unease.
Think about the last time you reached for your phone or a snack without deciding to. What happened just before? Was there a small moment of unease?

cards.title: Log a non-worry loop
cards.body: Log one loop today where the behavior isn't worrying: scrolling, snacking, searching, tidying or anything else. If it's not on the list, add your own.
Most of the time you notice a loop when it's already over: half an hour of worry gone, and the thought "Why did I do that again?"

cards.title: Late noticing still counts
cards.body: Spotting a loop afterward isn't a failure. It's how everyone starts. Each loop you notice after the fact trains your brain to notice the next one a little sooner.

cards.title: Earlier gives you room
cards.body: When you catch a loop at the trigger, or in its first minute, there's a small gap before the habit takes over. You don't need to do anything with that gap yet. Just knowing it's there changes things.

cards.title: Learn your early signs
cards.body: Loops often announce themselves: a tight jaw, a familiar "What if…", a hand already reaching for the phone. Learning your early signs is like learning the sound of your own front door.

cards.title: The first "What if…"
cards.body: Zara used to notice her money worry only after an hour of checking her bank app. This week she caught it at the first "What if…" while making coffee, and logged it right there, before the checking started.
What's usually the very first sign that one of your loops is starting? A thought, a feeling in your body, an action? Name one.

cards.title: Log a loop as it starts, not after
cards.body: Try to log a loop as it starts, while the trigger is still fresh. If you only catch it afterward, log it anyway, and notice how far in you were when you noticed.
Ten days ago, a loop was just something that happened to you. Now you can name its parts.

cards.title: You've built a skill
cards.body: Noticing a loop and naming its trigger, behavior and result is a real skill, and you've practiced it every day. It's the foundation for everything that comes next.

cards.title: Seeing is already changing it
cards.body: Some loops may already feel a little different. Catching one can take away some of its momentum. That isn't you trying harder. It's what happens when the brain sees a habit clearly.

cards.title: What comes next
cards.body: In stage 2 you'll look more closely at the result: what each habit really gives you. That's the part that lets a habit loosen on its own.

cards.title: Fourteen loops later
cards.body: Looking back over ten days, Ana saw she'd logged fourteen loops. Most were about work, and most started in the evening. She also noticed something new: twice this week she'd caught a loop early and let it pass.
Think back over the past week. What's one thing you've noticed about your loops that you didn't know ten days ago?

cards.title: Look back at your first ten days in Insights
cards.body: Open Insights and choose "Last 4 weeks." Look at how many loops you've noticed since you started, and which triggers come up most. Each one is a loop you saw, instead of one that just ran.
You finally put the phone down after twenty minutes of scrolling. Be honest: do you feel better than when you picked it up?

cards.title: Your brain keeps score
cards.body: Each time a behavior runs, your brain records what it got. If it scores the result as worth having, it nudges you to repeat the behavior next time. That score is what keeps a habit going.

cards.title: The score can be out of date
cards.body: Many scores were set long ago, sometimes in a single moment of relief. Worry may once have felt useful, so your brain still rates it highly, even if today it mostly leaves you tired.

cards.title: Update it by looking
cards.body: You can't argue a habit into changing its score. But you can let your brain see what the behavior gives you now, clearly and in the moment. That fresh information is what updates it.

cards.title: Twenty minutes of news
cards.body: Mia scrolls the news for twenty minutes whenever she feels uneasy, sure it will calm her down. Today she stopped afterwards and asked herself how she felt. The answer: more on edge than before. She'll probably check again tomorrow, but now part of her knows it doesn't help, and each time she notices, the pull gets a little weaker.
Recall a habit you did recently. Feel what it left you with, not what you think it should have left you with. Relief? Tension? Not much at all?

cards.title: Check the result honestly every time you log today
cards.body: Log every loop you notice today. At "What did it actually give you?", take one breath and pick what you really feel, even if that's "Not sure."

title: Worry is a habit, not a fact

cards.body: Your partner is late home, and within two minutes your mind has written a whole story: the accident, the hospital, the phone call. Then the door opens.

cards.title: Worry sounds certain
cards.body: Worried thoughts often arrive sounding sure: "This will go badly." "They're upset with me." The certainty is part of the habit. It feels like information, but it's a pattern your mind has practiced.

cards.title: Check the track record
cards.body: Think back over this month's worries. How many came true the way the worry said they would? Most people find very few did, and the ones that did were rarely helped by the worrying.

cards.title: A thought, not a fact
cards.body: You don't have to prove a worried thought wrong. You can simply see it as a thought: "There's the worry habit again." That small step back makes it easier to hold lightly.

cards.title: Two small edits
cards.body: Kofi spent the whole weekend convinced his boss would tear his report apart. On Monday the feedback was two small edits and "Thanks, good work." He made a note of it, and the next time the same worry came up, he recognized it.
Think of one thing you worried about last week. What did the worry predict? What actually happened?

cards.title: Note one worry that didn't come true
cards.body: Find one worry that didn't come true, or didn't turn out as badly as it said. Log it as a loop and add a few words in the note, like "didn't happen."
After an hour of replaying a conversation, you notice your shoulders are up near your ears and your jaw aches.

cards.title: The body keeps the receipts
cards.body: A habit's result isn't only a thought like "that didn't help." It's felt: tight shoulders, a heavy stomach, a buzzing chest, tired eyes. These sensations are often more honest than our opinions.

cards.title: Feeling it beats knowing it
cards.body: You can know that worry doesn't help and still worry. Feeling the tightness it leaves behind gives your brain the raw information it learns from, and that's what shifts the habit.

cards.title: A quick scan is enough
cards.body: You don't need a long exercise. After a loop, take a few seconds to scan from your head down to your stomach and ask: where do I feel this?

cards.title: A tight chest
cards.body: After checking her phone for messages over and over (behavior), Elena noticed a tight chest and shallow breathing (result). Naming the tightness made the habit's cost feel real in a way thinking about it never had.
Take a breath. Scan your forehead, jaw, shoulders, chest and stomach. Where is there tension right now? Just notice it. There's nothing to fix.

cards.title: Name where you feel a loop's result
cards.body: After the next loop you log, scan your body and name where you feel its result. Add it in the note, like "tight chest" or "heavy stomach."
"I'm not going to check again." Five minutes later you're checking again, and now you're annoyed with yourself too.

cards.title: Fighting feeds the loop
cards.body: Pushing a habit away takes effort, and effort runs out, especially when you're tired or stressed, which is exactly when loops show up. And when willpower gives way, blaming yourself often becomes a new loop.

cards.title: Get interested instead
cards.body: Instead of fighting the urge, you can get interested in it. What does it feel like? Where is it in your body? Does it change as you watch it? Curiosity takes far less effort than resisting.

cards.title: You don't have to stop yet
cards.body: This stage isn't about stopping anything. If you end up doing the habit, that's fine. Do it with your eyes open, and notice what it gives you.

cards.title: Looking up symptoms
cards.body: Ravi's doctor had checked the twinge and told him it was nothing to worry about. Still, whenever he felt it, he'd search his symptoms online. Even after reading it was probably nothing, he'd worry his last search had missed something, so he searched again, and again. For weeks he tried to force himself to stop, and kept giving in. This week he tried something different: when the urge came, he got curious about it instead of fighting it. He noticed how it felt: restless, a pull in his hands. Sometimes he searched anyway. But a few times the urge faded before he'd even picked up his phone.
Think of a habit that tugs at you. Picture the urge arriving. Instead of saying no to it, ask: "What does this urge feel like right now?"

cards.title: Notice one urge without fighting it
cards.body: When an urge comes, watch it for a few breaths. Whatever you do next, log the loop.
The first time you notice that checking the news makes you feel worse, it's a small surprise. By the tenth time, the habit starts to feel less tempting.

cards.title: Each look counts
cards.body: One honest look at a result won't undo a habit built over years. But each look adds to your brain's tally. Over time the habit's appeal fades on its own, without a fight.

cards.title: Start with your most common loop
cards.body: The loops you repeat most carry the highest score in your brain. They also give you the most chances to look, so they're where change tends to show first.

cards.title: Patience, not pressure
cards.body: Habits don't drop away in a day. Some days the pull will feel just as strong as ever. That's normal, and the looking is still working underneath.

cards.title: The budget spreadsheet
cards.body: Hana's most common loop was money worry (trigger) followed by reopening her budget spreadsheet (behavior). She started paying close attention to what it gave her each time. After two weeks she reached for the spreadsheet less, and when she did, she stopped sooner.
What's your most common loop? If you're not sure, Insights shows your top triggers and your most common habit.

cards.title: Check the result of your most common loop
cards.body: The next time your most common loop shows up, log it and check its result carefully. Take a breath before you choose, and feel what it really gave you.
You've locked the door. You go back to check. It's locked. On the way to the car, you wonder whether you checked properly.

cards.title: Checking promises certainty
cards.body: Re-checking the door, your messages, the weather or your bank balance promises one thing: certainty. "Once I know for sure, I'll relax."

cards.title: Certainty doesn't stick
cards.body: The relief from a check is real, but it fades fast, often within minutes. Then the doubt comes back, and the urge to check comes with it. Each check can make the next one feel more necessary.

cards.title: Watch the fade
cards.body: You don't need to stop checking today. Instead, watch how long the relief lasts. Seeing it fade, again and again, helps your brain update what checking is worth.

cards.title: Refresh, refresh
cards.body: Waiting to hear back about a job (trigger), Ben refreshed his email every few minutes (behavior). Each refresh brought a flicker of hope, then a drop. When he paid attention, the calm from each check lasted less than a minute (result).
Think of something you tend to check more than once. The last time you checked it, how long did the calm last?

cards.title: Catch one re-checking loop
cards.body: When you catch one, log it with "Kept checking," and at the result, notice how long the relief actually lasted.
You catch yourself worrying again, and straight away another voice joins in: "Why can't you just stop? What's wrong with you?"

cards.title: The second loop
cards.body: Many people stack a second loop on top of the first. The trigger is noticing the habit. The behavior is criticizing yourself. The result is usually more tension, which feeds the next round of worry.

cards.title: Criticism makes a promise too
cards.body: Like worry, self-judgment promises something: "If I'm hard on myself, I'll do better." Check whether it keeps that promise. For most people, it mostly leaves them feeling smaller and more stuck.

cards.title: Treat it like any other loop
cards.body: You don't need to argue with the critical voice. Treat it like any other habit: name it, notice what set it off, and see what it really gives you.

cards.title: "A terrible parent"
cards.body: Lucia snapped at her son, then spent the evening telling herself she was a terrible parent (behavior). By bedtime she felt heavy and exhausted, and no closer to the calm talk she wanted to have with him (result).
Think of the last time you criticized yourself. What were the words? What tone of voice? How did your body feel afterward?

cards.title: Log a self-criticism loop
cards.body: Log one self-criticism loop today. If it isn't in your list of behaviors, add your own, like "Criticized myself."
It doesn't feel like much is changing. Then one evening you realize you haven't checked your work email since dinner.

cards.title: Change is quiet
cards.body: Habits rarely change in big moments. They shift in small ones: a loop that's a little shorter, an urge that fades on its own, a moment you notice sooner. These are easy to miss.

cards.title: Your logs remember
cards.body: Every result you've logged is a record of what your habits give you. Looking back can show a change your day-to-day memory missed.

cards.title: Count what you see, not what you stop
cards.body: Success here isn't fewer loops. Logging more can simply mean you're noticing more. What counts is that you're seeing clearly.

cards.title: What overthinking gave
cards.body: Omar felt like nothing had changed. Then he looked at what "Overthought it" had given him over the past two weeks: more worry, nearly every time. Seeing it in one place made something click: "That habit really isn't doing what I thought."
Think of one small change in the past week. A loop caught sooner? An urge that passed? It counts.

cards.title: Look at what your habits gave you in Insights
cards.body: Open Insights and look at your most common habit: what has it given you? Notice how it feels to see that in one place.
You worried about the tax deadline, so you sat down and filed. The worry went away. Was that a loop?

cards.title: Not every response is a trap
cards.body: Sometimes unease leads you to act, and the action solves the problem. Making a plan, sending the email, booking the appointment: these can be genuinely helpful.

cards.title: The difference is in the result
cards.body: A helpful response usually ends something. The problem gets handled, and the worry eases and stays eased. A loop tends to repeat: the same thoughts, the same checks, nothing new happening.

cards.title: Honest both ways
cards.body: This isn't about calling everything you do a bad habit. It's about seeing clearly. When something helps, notice that too, and pick "It actually helped."

cards.title: Two things to say
cards.body: Grace was dreading a hard conversation with her sister. She wrote down the two things she wanted to say and called that evening. The worry eased and didn't come back. The same week she noticed another pattern: rehearsing arguments in the shower, which never led anywhere.
Think of something you did about a worry recently. Did it end something, or did the worry come back soon after?

cards.title: Sort one loop: helpful or not?
cards.body: Log one loop and sort it honestly. If it really helped, choose "It actually helped." If it didn't, notice what it gave you instead.
Some habits still pull at you. But a few may feel a little less shiny than they did ten days ago.

cards.title: The shine wears off
cards.body: When you keep seeing what a habit really gives you, its appeal slowly fades, a bit like a song you've heard too many times. You don't decide to stop liking it. It just loses its pull.

cards.title: Not all at once
cards.body: Some habits loosen quickly. Others take longer, especially the ones you've practiced for years. Both are normal, and the looking is still working.

cards.title: What comes next
cards.body: In stage 3 you'll use four tools that give your brain something better to do when a loop starts: curiosity, breathing, noting and kindness. They work best now, after you've seen what the old habits really give you.

cards.title: The letdown coming
cards.body: Nikhil noticed that "Searched online" no longer felt like relief. He still did it sometimes, but now he could feel the letdown coming before he'd even opened the browser.
Which habit feels a little less rewarding now than when you started? What changed in how you see it?

cards.title: Log the habit that's lost the most shine
cards.body: Pick the habit that feels least rewarding now. The next time it shows up, log it and take your time at "What did it actually give you?" Notice whether it pulls at you the way it used to.
Think of the last time you were really curious about something: a mystery, a new place, a puzzle. Notice how different that feels from worry.

cards.title: Your brain wants a better offer
cards.body: Your brain repeats what feels rewarding. If worry is the best response it knows to unease, it will keep choosing worry. Changing the habit is easier when there's something on offer that genuinely feels better.

cards.title: Curiosity is that offer
cards.body: Curiosity is open and interested. Worry is narrow and tight. When you turn curiosity toward an anxious feeling ("Hmm, what is this?"), you're no longer stuck inside it. You're exploring it.

cards.title: You already have it
cards.body: You don't need to learn curiosity. You already have it. The skill is pointing it at the feeling in your body instead of at the worried story.

cards.title: "Hmm, what is this?"
cards.body: In a stressful meeting, Rosa felt the familiar knot in her stomach. Instead of running through everything that could go wrong, she asked herself, "Hmm, what is this? Where exactly is it?" The knot didn't vanish, but she felt less caught up in it.
Notice any feeling in your body right now, even a small one. Say "Hmm…" and get interested in it. Is it warm or cool? Still or moving?

cards.title: Use Get curious once
cards.body: The next time a loop starts, open Get curious and follow it to the end. Afterward, notice how you feel.
"Anxious" sounds like one solid thing. Up close it's more like weather: a flutter here, a tightness there, a wave of heat that comes and goes.

cards.title: Feelings are made of parts
cards.body: An anxious feeling is built from smaller sensations: pressure, tingling, warmth, a tight band. Taken as a whole it can feel overwhelming. Taken piece by piece, each part is easier to be with.

cards.title: Nothing stays the same
cards.body: Watch a sensation closely and you'll often see it change. It moves, grows, shrinks or fades. That's worth knowing: what feels permanent is actually always shifting.

cards.title: Details keep you here
cards.body: Looking closely at a sensation keeps your attention in your body, right now, rather than in a worried story about later.

cards.title: Three sensations
cards.body: Before a flight, Felix felt "panicky." When he looked closely, he found three things: a fluttering in his stomach, tingling hands and a tight throat. The fluttering came in waves. The tingling faded after a few minutes.
Pick one sensation in your body. Notice its size and its edges. Is it moving? Watch it for three breaths and see whether anything changes.

cards.title: Get curious about one body sensation
cards.body: When you feel anxious today, use Get curious on one body sensation. Notice its details, and whether it changes as you watch.
A thought on its own can sweep you away. A thought with a label, like "planning" or "worrying," is something you can see.

cards.title: Naming makes space
cards.body: When you name what's happening ("thinking," "tight," "worrying"), you shift from being inside the experience to watching it. The thought is still there, but now there's a little room around it.

cards.title: Simple words work best
cards.body: You don't need the perfect word. "Thinking" is fine. "Something" is fine. The point isn't accuracy. It's the small act of noticing and naming.

cards.title: Again and again
cards.body: Thoughts and feelings keep coming, and that's fine. Each time something new shows up, name it. Every label is a small step back.

cards.title: Planning, worrying, planning
cards.body: Lying awake, Amara's mind raced from work to money to a friend's birthday. She began naming each one quietly: "planning… worrying… planning… remembering." The thoughts kept coming, but she felt less swept along by them.
For the next few breaths, name whatever shows up: "thinking," "hearing," "itchy," "worrying." One word each time. There's no need to get it right.

cards.title: Use Note it during a loop
cards.body: The next time you're caught in a loop, open Note it and tap a word each time you notice something. Keep going for a minute or two.
Before a hard phone call, you notice your breath is fast and high in your chest, as if you're already running.

cards.title: Breath talks to the body
cards.body: Anxiety speeds the breath up. Slowing it down, especially the out-breath, sends the opposite signal: there's no emergency right now.

cards.title: An anchor, not a fix
cards.body: Slow breathing won't make worry disappear. Think of it as an anchor: something steady to come back to when your thoughts start pulling you away.

cards.title: Before helps too
cards.body: Breathing helps in the middle of a loop, and it also helps just before a moment you know will be hard. A minute or two beforehand can take the edge off.

cards.title: Ten minutes to ten
cards.body: Chris had a presentation at 10. At 9:50 they sat in a quiet corner and used Breathe for two minutes: in for four, out for six. Their heart was still beating fast when they began, but they felt steady enough to start.
Breathe in through your nose for a count of four, then out slowly for a count of six. Repeat four times, paying special attention to the out-breath.

cards.title: Use Breathe before a stressful moment
cards.body: Think of a moment today that might be stressful: a meeting, a call, a conversation. Use Breathe for a minute or two just before it.
When a friend is struggling, you probably know just what to say. When it's you, the words that come out are often much harsher.

cards.title: Judgment is a habit too
cards.body: As you saw on day 17, self-criticism runs as a loop. It promises to make you better and mostly gives back tension and low mood.

cards.title: Kindness is a better offer
cards.body: Being kind to yourself isn't letting yourself off the hook. It's treating yourself the way you'd treat someone you care about who's having a hard time. It also feels better, which is exactly why your brain can learn to prefer it.

cards.title: Awkward at first is normal
cards.body: If kindness toward yourself feels strange, or even untrue, that's common. It's a new habit, and like any new habit it gets easier with practice.

cards.title: A missed deadline
cards.body: After missing an important deadline, Yuki heard the usual "You're useless." She paused, rested a hand on her chest and said quietly, "This is hard right now. Lots of people feel this way. I can be gentle with myself." The criticism didn't vanish, but it loosened its grip.
Think of a recent moment you were hard on yourself. What would you say to a friend in the same spot? Say it to yourself, silently, in the same tone.

cards.title: Use Be kind after a self-critical loop
cards.body: The next time you catch yourself in a self-critical loop, open Be kind and go through it. Afterward, notice how it feels compared with the criticism.
The urge to check your phone feels like it will keep growing until you give in. Does it, though?

cards.title: Urges are waves
cards.body: An urge builds, peaks and then falls, often within a few minutes. It feels as if it will keep growing forever, but it doesn't. The catch is that we usually act at the peak, so we never get to see it fall.

cards.title: Ride it, don't fight it
cards.body: You don't have to push the urge away. Watch it the way a surfer watches a wave: notice it build, feel its strongest point, and see it start to ease.

cards.title: Every wave teaches something
cards.body: Each time you watch an urge pass without acting on it, your brain learns that urges aren't orders. They come and go on their own.

cards.title: "Are we OK?"
cards.body: Jack felt a strong pull to text his partner "Are we OK?" for the third time that day. He set a five-minute timer and watched the urge instead. It peaked around the second minute as a tight, restless feeling in his chest. By the fifth minute it was much quieter.
Think of an urge you feel often. Imagine it arriving, and picture it as a wave: building, peaking, then slowly settling. Breathe as you watch it.

cards.title: Watch one urge pass
cards.body: The next time an urge shows up, ride it for a few minutes before you act. Use Breathe if it helps. Notice whether it rises and falls.
You now have four tools. When a loop starts, which one do you reach for?

cards.title: Tools fit moments
cards.body: Each tool suits a different kind of moment. Get curious helps when a feeling is strong and physical. Breathe helps when you're keyed up, or before something stressful. Note it helps when your mind is busy and racing. Be kind helps when you're being hard on yourself.

cards.title: Decide ahead
cards.body: Choosing in the middle of a loop is hard. Deciding ahead of time ("When work worry starts, I'll use Breathe") makes it much easier to follow through.

cards.title: Your experience is the guide
cards.body: Think about which tools have left you feeling lighter. Your own results are a better guide than any general rule.

cards.title: Bedtime worry
cards.body: Leila's top trigger was "Trying to sleep." She'd noticed that Note it settled her mind more than breathing did. So she decided: when bedtime worry starts, she'll tap words for two minutes instead of lying there replaying the day.
Think about your top trigger. Which of the four tools seems the best fit for it, and why?

cards.title: Pick a tool for your top trigger
cards.body: Check your top trigger in Insights and choose a go-to tool for it. The next time that trigger shows up, use the tool and notice how you feel afterward.
You've had a good stretch. Then one bad night, and the old worry is back as if it never left.

cards.title: Old paths don't vanish
cards.body: A habit you've practiced for years leaves a well-worn path. Even after you've built new ones, the old path is still there, and stress, tiredness or a big change can send you down it.

cards.title: A return isn't a reset
cards.body: When an old loop comes back, it can feel as if all your progress is gone. It isn't. What you've learned about seeing loops clearly is still there, and you'll often notice sooner and recover faster than before.

cards.title: Plan on a good day
cards.body: The best time to prepare for a bad day is on a good one. Pick the tool you'll reach for first, and keep a kind phrase ready in Be kind, so it's there when the harsh voice comes back.

cards.title: A rough week
cards.body: After a family argument, Marcus had a rough week, and his worry came back strong. He fell back on what he'd set up: log the loops, use Breathe at night, and read the phrase he'd kept in Be kind, "I'm doing the best I can with what I have." By the weekend he felt steadier, and less shaken than he'd expected.
Think about what usually makes your worry worse: stress, poor sleep, a certain kind of news. Which is most likely to bring an old loop back?

cards.title: Keep a kind phrase for a bad day
cards.body: Go through Be kind and keep one phrase that feels true to you. On a hard day you'll find it under Your phrases. Then decide which tool you'll reach for first. If anxiety ever feels much harder than usual, or stays that way, open Help for support lines.
Think back to day 1. Loops just happened to you. Now you can often see one coming.

cards.title: Memory isn't a fair judge
cards.body: On an anxious day it's easy to believe nothing has changed, because memory leans on how you feel today. Your logs are a fairer record.

cards.title: What to look for
cards.body: Compare your weeks. You may have logged more loops as you got better at noticing, or fewer as some loosened. Look at what your common habits gave you, and how you felt after using the tools.

cards.title: Progress isn't a straight line
cards.body: Some weeks are harder than others. A rough week near the end doesn't erase what came before. Look at the overall direction.

cards.title: Week 1 and week 4
cards.body: Ines compared her first and fourth weeks. She'd logged about the same number of loops, but in week 1 most were "Overthought it" followed by "More worry." In week 4 she'd used Get curious and Breathe several times, and felt lighter after most of them.
Before you look: what's one thing you think has changed since day 1?

cards.title: Compare week 1 and week 4 in Insights
cards.body: Open Insights, choose "Last 4 weeks" and compare your first week with this one. Notice what's different, and what's the same.
Thirty days ago you started with one idea: anxiety can run like a habit. You've spent a month learning to see it.

cards.title: What you've learned
cards.body: You can spot a loop's trigger, behavior and result. You've seen what your habits really give you. And you have four tools that offer your brain something better.

cards.title: Keep it light
cards.body: The course ends, but the skills work best with small, regular use: logging a loop when you notice one, and reaching for a tool when worry shows up. A few minutes a day is plenty.

cards.title: Come back any time
cards.body: All thirty lessons stay here. Revisit one when a loop feels stuck or you'd like a refresher. Home will suggest one now and then.

cards.title: One habit kept
cards.body: Theo kept one habit from the course: logging a loop whenever he caught one, then following it with a minute of Breathe. Months later he still did it a few times a week, and his evenings felt more like his own again.
Of everything in the course, what's the one thing you most want to keep doing?

cards.title: Check your daily check-in
cards.body: It's in Settings. Keep it, move it to a time that suits life after the course, or turn it off if you'd rather come back on your own.
